title: Person overboard
about: Person overboard from a small boat in New Zealand: shout, throw, watch, stop, call for help, recover, warm, report. Keeps the times.

sources.name: Coastguard New Zealand, "What to do in an emergency" (main source)
Greater Wellington Regional Council Harbours, "Wellington Skippers Cockpit Guide" (First edition, January 2023)
Northland Regional Council, "Distress, urgency and calls"
Maritime New Zealand, "Surviving in cold water"
Water Safety New Zealand, "Cold water survival"
Tasman District Council (Harbourmaster), "Maritime accidents and responsibilities"
NOT NZ: Safe Transport Victoria (Australia), Recreational Boating Safety Handbook, "Person Overboard"
NOT NZ: Royal Yachting Association (UK), "Man overboard"

warning: Emergency: VHF Channel 16 or call 111. Best used by a crew member who is not steering or watching the person. Lines marked AU guide or UK guide are not New Zealand guidance.
audience: Skippers and crew of small recreational boats in New Zealand
version: Coastguard NZ 'What to do in an emergency' (no date, footer 2026); Maritime NZ 'Radio a MAYDAY' (no date); Wellington Skippers Cockpit Guide (First edition, January 2023); Northland RC 'Distress, urgency and calls' (no date); Maritime NZ 'Surviving in cold water' (no date); Water Safety NZ 'Cold water survival' (no date, footer 2026); Tasman DC 'Maritime accidents and responsibilities' (no date); NOT NZ: Safe Transport Victoria 'Person Overboard' (last modified 31 Jul 2023); NOT NZ: RYA 'Man overboard' (last updated 29 Oct 2025); all read 21 Nov 2026

lines.text: Shout loudly so everyone knows.

quotes.text: Shout loudly, to make sure everyone knows that someone's gone overboard

lines.text: Person went overboard
Tap the buttons as you go: the app keeps the times.
Wellington guide: shout to alert the skipper.

quotes.text: Shout - to alert the skipper.

options.label: They are already back on board

lines.text: Throw a life buoy, line or lifejacket as close as you can to them.

quotes.text: Throw a life buoy, line or lifejacket as close as you can to the person, not only to help them stay afloat but also to mark their position

lines.text: Flotation thrown
Avoid jumping in. If you must, take a flotation device.

quotes.text: Avoid jumping in the water if possible. If you must, ensure that you take a flotation device to offer support if you get tired.

lines.text: It helps them float and marks where they are. Wellington guide: things that float make a path back and give them something to grab.

quotes.text: Throw - things that float to make a path back and gives the person in the water something to grab onto.

lines.text: Don't take your eyes off them. Keep pointing.

quotes.text: Watch the person carefully - it's easy to lose sight of someone in the water, so don't take your eyes off them!
Point - keep pointing in the direction of the person in the water, even if you can't see them.

lines.text: AU guide: ask one person on board to point continuously, so others can get gear ready.

quotes.text: Ask someone on board to point continuously at the person in the water for the reference of others on board who may be preparing equipment or other head-down activities.

options.label: No, we lost sight of them

lines.text: Keep pointing where they were, even if you can't see them.

quotes.text: Point - keep pointing in the direction of the person in the water, even if you can't see them.

lines.text: Lost sight of person
The sources do not say how to search. The next screens are stop, turn back and mark the position.
Stop the boat and turn back as soon as you're able.

quotes.text: Stop the boat and turn back as soon as you're able.

lines.text: Boat stopped, turning back
The propeller is a danger to anyone in the water.

quotes.text: Remember that the prop is always a danger to anyone in the water, so take care as you approach them.

lines.text: AU guide: if they are close, motor in neutral and swing the propeller away from them.

quotes.text: If the person overboard is close to the vessel put the motor in neutral, raise the alarm and swing the propeller quickly away from them.

lines.text: No New Zealand source names a way to turn back.
Where the person went in

quotes.text: If operating with a GPS or chart plotter it may be possible to quickly create a waypoint where the event occurred.
Press the man overboard button on the plotter to provide a last known position

lines.text: If you have crew, one person keeps pointing while another taps the GPS button.
Coastguard NZ: the flotation you threw also marks their position.

quotes.text: but also to mark their position

lines.text: AU guide: check your bearings on landmarks; a waypoint on a GPS or chart plotter helps if a search is needed. UK guide: press the man overboard button on the plotter.

quotes.text: Check your bearings relative to any prominent landmarks.
These will assist if a search is required.

lines.text: Marking the position on GPS comes only from the AU and UK guides; no New Zealand source mentions it.
Coastguard NZ: a person overboard is an example of a Mayday (grave and imminent danger).

quotes.text: A distress/Mayday call is used to indicate that a boat or person is threatened by grave and imminent danger and requires immediate assistance
for example, a boat taking on water, a vessel on fire, a person overboard or a serious medical emergency such as a heart attack.

lines.text: Hand this phone to someone who is not steering or watching the person.
Wellington and Northland describe Pan-pan for urgent problems with no immediate danger. No source gives Pan-pan wording.

quotes.text: Pan-pan: Urgent situation with NO immediate danger (engine failure, drifting safely etc).
Note: when MAYDAY is not warranted but urgency is required for the safety of a vessel or person, PAN PAN should be used.

lines.text: How long someone lasts in the water (the sources differ; none is a countdown). Wellington guide: 1-3 hours with a life jacket on, around 10 minutes without.

quotes.text: you will survive 1-3 hours in the water with a life jacket on and around 10 minutes without.

lines.text: Maritime NZ: even a fit person can drown in cold water in under 10 minutes.

quotes.text: drown in under 10 minutes, long before hypothermia sets in.

lines.text: UK guide: crews have, on average, less than 11 minutes to recover someone from cold water before they become unresponsive.

quotes.text: less than 11 minutes to recover a crewmate who has fallen overboard into cold water before the victim becomes unresponsive.

lines.text: Coastguard's four steps do not say when to call for help.

options.label: No radio or phone: other signals
Not calling yet, or already called: go back to them

lines.text: Lifejacket on. Set off your distress beacon if you carry one.

quotes.text: Wear your lifejacket and activate your distress beacon (if carried on your vessel).

lines.text: Beacon activated
Radio on full power. Channel 16.

quotes.text: Switch your radio on to full power and turn to:
VHF: channel 16

lines.text: Coastguard NZ: or another local VHF channel you know is being monitored.

quotes.text: or another local VHF channel you know is being monitored

lines.text: SSB radio: 2182kHZ, 4125kHZ, 6215kHZ or 8291kHZ.

quotes.text: SSB: 2182kHZ, 4125kHZ, 6215kHZ or 8291kHZ

lines.text: UK guide: issue a MAYDAY or DSC alert.

quotes.text: issue a MAYDAY or DSC Alert.

lines.text: "Mayday. Mayday. Mayday."

quotes.text: Mayday. Mayday. Mayday.

lines.text: "This is [boat], [boat], [boat], [call sign]."

quotes.text: This is Achiever, Achiever, Achiever ZMW3545.
"This is [vessel name]" 3 times

lines.text: "Mayday, [boat] [call sign]."

quotes.text: Mayday, Achiever ZMW3545.

lines.text: "We are at (state your general geographical position) in position (latitude & longitude)."

quotes.text: We are at (state your general geographical position) in position (latitude & longitude).

lines.text: "We have (state what is wrong, the nature of your distress)."

quotes.text: We have (state what is wrong, the nature of your distress).

lines.text: "We require immediate assistance."

quotes.text: We require immediate assistance.

lines.text: "We have (state how many people on-board)."

quotes.text: We have (state how many people on-board).

lines.text: Any other helpful information. "Over."

quotes.text: Any other helpful information.
Over.

lines.text: Position to read out
Mayday sent
App's note: here, what is wrong is a person overboard.
This is Coastguard NZ's example call; put your own details in the brackets.
Maritime NZ: position can be latitude and longitude, or bearing and distance from a known landmark.

quotes.text: [vessel's latitude and longitude OR bearing and distance from a known landmark]

lines.text: Maritime NZ: other information can include a description of your boat, and any liferaft or dinghy.

quotes.text: [any other information, e.g. number of persons on board, description of vessel, liferaft or dinghy

lines.text: Wait a short time. Listen on the same channel.

quotes.text: wait a short time for a reply, listening on the same frequency for an acknowledgement.

lines.text: Coastguard Radio, Maritime Radio or a nearby boat may answer.

quotes.text: Wait for a response from either Coastguard Radio or Maritime Radio (or a nearby vessel).

lines.text: Repeat the Mayday. If needed, try every distress frequency on your radio.

quotes.text: repeat the MAYDAY distress call
if needed, work through all the distress frequencies on your radio and repeat the call.

options.label: Go back to the person now

lines.text: Follow their instructions. Tell them if you set off an EPIRB or PLB.

quotes.text: follow their instructions.
tell them you have activated your EPIRB or PLB if you have one

lines.text: Reply received
Description of the person
Coastguard NZ: they will ask for more information and confirm help is being sent.

quotes.text: They will then ask for more information and confirm assistance is being sent to you as soon as possible.

options.label: Still in the water: go back to them

lines.text: Call 111 from your mobile. Ask for Police.

quotes.text: call 111 from your mobile phone and ask for Police.

lines.text: *500: the sources disagree on using it for emergencies (see More).

quotes.text: For non-urgent assistance such as an electrical problem or mechanical issue, call our Operations Centre on *500 from your mobile phone.
All emergency distress calls - VHF channel 16 or phone *500

lines.text: 111 called
Description of the person
Coastguard NZ: Police will task Coastguard.

quotes.text: You can either call 111 and Police will task Coastguard with responding

lines.text: Coastguard NZ and the Wellington guide say *500 is for non-urgent help. A Northland page lists *500 for emergency calls too.

quotes.text: For non-urgent assistance such as an electrical problem or mechanical issue, call our Operations Centre on *500 from your mobile phone.
All emergency distress calls - VHF channel 16 or phone *500

options.label: Still in the water: go back to them

lines.text: Raise and lower outstretched arms. Sound a horn. Red flare. SOS.

quotes.text: Slowly and repeatedly raising and lowering your arms outstretched to each side.
Continuously sounding a fog horn or siren.
Using a hand-held flare or parachute flare showing a red light.
Signalling SOS by any signal method, including sound, light or mirror.

lines.text: Use these signals only to show you are in distress.

quotes.text: Use these signals only to indicate distress

lines.text: Distress signal used

Northland RC: SOS by sound, light or mirror is three shorts, three longs, three shorts. Arms: slowly and repeatedly, to each side. Horn or siren: continuously. Flare: hand-held or parachute, red light.

quotes.text: The SOS signal is: three shorts, three longs, three shorts.

options.label: Still in the water: go back to them

lines.text: Take care with the propeller as you approach.

quotes.text: Remember that the prop is always a danger to anyone in the water, so take care as you approach them.

lines.text: UK guide: get recovery gear ready, tell them you are coming back, and come up upwind so the boat drifts towards them. Brief the crew on your next steps.

quotes.text: Prepare your recovery equipment and reassure the casualty that you will be returning to them.
Aim to position your vessel upwind of them, so that as you slow down the vessel is blown towards them.
Always ensure the crew is properly briefed on your next steps during recovery.

lines.text: No New Zealand source says how to approach.
Keep pointing where they were, even if you can't see them.

quotes.text: Point - keep pointing in the direction of the person in the water, even if you can't see them.

lines.text: Lost sight of person
The sources do not say how to search. If you marked the position, it is in the Log.
AU and UK guides: engine in neutral or off.

quotes.text: Position the vessel to bring the person alongside then stop engines to avoid striking them with a spinning propeller.
Once alongside the casualty, it's important to ensure that engines are left in neutral or switched off.

lines.text: The propeller must not hit them.

quotes.text: Regardless, risk to the casualty from a spinning propellor must be avoided at all costs.

lines.text: UK guide: whether you switch off depends on the weather, your boat and other things. It is the skipper's call.

quotes.text: Whether or not you switch off the engine depends on weather conditions, your vessel, or a variety of other factors.

lines.text: New Zealand sources only say take care with the prop.
Use the boat hook to help recover them.

quotes.text: your boat hook can be used for checking the depth of water, pushing off, or helping recover a person overboard.

lines.text: AU guide: bring them in over the stern if you can; a small boat may capsize over the side.

quotes.text: Help the person into the vessel, preferably over the stern, as a small vessel might capsize or take on water if you try taking them in over the side.

lines.text: AU guide: a ladder helps them get back on board.

quotes.text: It is recommended that your vessel is fitted with a ladder or that you carry a portable ladder to help with reboarding a person in the water.

lines.text: UK guide: if they are awake and can help, throw a heaving line.

quotes.text: If the casualty is conscious and can assist in their recovery, throw a heaving line to help recover them.

lines.text: No New Zealand source says more about getting them on board than the boat hook.
AU guide: someone who can't help themselves is hard to get back in.

quotes.text: If they cannot help themselves, it is difficult to get them back into the vessel.

lines.text: UK guide: if unconscious, crew reaching overboard are at risk too.

quotes.text: A crew member will need to secure a lifting device to the casualty's lifejacket or harness. In this situation, other crew members will be at risk reaching overboard or being lowered towards the casualty to make contact.

lines.text: UK guide: a scramble net, ladder, or swim platform on the stern (calm conditions only) can help. If they are unconscious, a crew member fixes a lifting device to their lifejacket or harness.

quotes.text: A scramble net, rescue ladder, boarding ladder, or swim platform on the stern (calm conditions only) can be useful in helping to recover a man overboard.

lines.text: UK guide: lift them lying flat if you can, but drowning is the main risk, so getting them on board comes first.

quotes.text: When lifting a casualty onboard, they should remain in a horizontal position to avoid the potential medical complications caused by hydrostatic squeeze. However, drowning remains the primary risk, therefore recovery onboard is the priority.

options.label: Still in the water: call for help

lines.text: Person back on board
Watch them carefully. They may be hurt, cold or exhausted.

quotes.text: A person recovered from the water may be hurt, cold or exhausted.
Once the casualty is onboard, they need to be carefully monitored.

lines.text: These are the AU guide (hurt, cold or exhausted) and the UK guide (monitor; first aid; for someone not breathing or unconscious, all the appropriate steps). None of these sources gives first aid steps.

quotes.text: First aid needs to be provided and for non-breathing or unconscious casualties all the appropriate steps should be taken.

ask.question: Do they need help now (not breathing, unconscious or hurt)?

options.label: No, or help is already called: warm them

lines.text: Call VHF Channel 16, or 111 and ask for Police.

quotes.text: If your boat is sinking, someone is injured or life is in danger, immediately call VHF Channel 16 (the international maritime distress channel) or another local VHF channel you know is being monitored, or call 111 from your mobile phone and ask for Police.

lines.text: Take off all wet clothing. Wrap them in dry clothing or blankets.

quotes.text: Remove all wet clothing and warm the person by wrapping them in dry clothing or blankets.

lines.text: Get them out of the wind.

quotes.text: Get out of the water and the wind as soon as possible to keep warm.

lines.text: UK guide: they should be checked at a medical facility (risk of secondary drowning). No NZ source says this.

quotes.text: Wet clothing should be removed, and the casualty should be warmed, carefully monitored, and transported to a medical facility for review.
Conscious casualties or those who have recovered themselves are at risk of shock, hypothermia, secondary drowning, and injuries incurred during their fall or recovery.

lines.text: Wellington guide: children lose body heat much faster than adults.

quotes.text: Kids lose body heat much faster than adults.

lines.text: UK guide: they are also at risk of shock, hypothermia and injuries from the fall or recovery.

quotes.text: Conscious casualties or those who have recovered themselves are at risk of shock, hypothermia, secondary drowning, and injuries incurred during their fall or recovery.

lines.text: No longer need help? Cancel the call.

quotes.text: Calls and messages must be cancelled if assistance is no longer required or when the incident is over.

lines.text: Help call cancelled
The sources don't say how to cancel a Mayday or a beacon you set off on purpose.
Wellington's 0508 472 269 is only for a beacon set off by accident.

quotes.text: If you accidentally activate your PLB or EPIRB, call 0508 472 269 or Maritime Radio on VHF 16.

lines.text: The Log shows what you called and when.
Report to Maritime Radio (VHF 16) or RCCNZ (0508 222 433) straight away.

quotes.text: You must also report any accident or incident to Maritime Radio on VHF 16 or RCCNZ on 0508 222 433 immediately

lines.text: Reported to Maritime Radio or RCCNZ
Report to Maritime NZ on their website forms within 24 hours.

quotes.text: and to Maritime NZ on the forms available from their website within 24 hours.
You'll need to contact Maritime NZ to report any accident.

lines.text: Reported to Maritime NZ
These come from one regional harbourmaster page (Tasman). If you made a Mayday, Maritime Radio may already know; the page does not say whether that counts as reporting.
The harbourmaster must also be told about a collision, sinking, grounding, a dangerous boat, an obstruction or damage to a navigation aid.

quotes.text: The master of any vessel (recreational or commercial) must report to the Harbourmaster as soon as practicable if:

lines.text: Show rescuers the Log: the times, the position and the description you typed.
Anything else to hand over
This list is the app's summary. No source lists what to record after a person overboard, or says to note the time.
Keep this phone's Log. Do what Coastguard, Police or Maritime NZ tell you.
